## Minister. Mother. Leader.
Sarah’s call to service continues. She is the only Democrat in Iowa over the past few years who has consistently won competitive elections in Republican districts, and now she is running for Congress in IA-03 to ensure Iowans have a voice in Washington. Her journey from service worker to minister, nonprofit leader, and state legislator is a testament to her unwavering commitment to public service and the people of Iowa.

pages.title: Issues - Sarah for Iowa
pages.text:
## Standing up for hardworking Iowans
Iowans are tired of broken promises, rising costs, and politicians who are more interested in scoring partisan victories than solving real problems. I’ve spent my life showing up for people — as a chaplain, a pastor, a community leader, and a state senator. In Congress, I’ll do what I’ve always done: stand up for hardworking Iowans, deliver results, and work to protect your freedom, your paycheck, and your future.

pages.title: Immigration that’s smart, fair, and reflects our values - Sarah for Iowa
pages.text:
## Immigration that’s smart, fair, and reflects our values
Our immigration system is broken, and Washington is making the problem worse—chaos at the border, dysfunction in the courts, and politicians deeply out of touch with the needs of our communities. Iowa is stronger because of the people who’ve made a home here and contributed to our community. But we also need a system that enforces the law and secures our borders. In Congress, I’ll push for comprehensive immigration reform that fixes our broken system: secures the border, streamlines legal pathways, protects Dreamers, and invests in preventing human trafficking and drug smuggling. We also need to ensure ICE is following the law, accountable to the American people, and protecting, not hurting, our communities. It’s long past time for solutions, not politics as usual, because the status quo is failing everyone.

pages.title: A Higher Standard for Washington - Sarah for Iowa
pages.text:
## A Higher Standard for Washington
A lot of Iowans have given up on Washington. And it’s not hard to see why.
Members of Congress get rich off stock trades the rest of us could never make. Politicians spend decades in the same seat, cashing checks from the very corporations they’re supposed to keep an eye on. The President, members of Congress, and even Supreme Court justices play by a different set of rules than everyone else. It’s wrong. And I’m frustrated about it, same as you.
I’m running because public service is supposed to mean serving the public, not yourself, not your donors, not your party. Somewhere along the way, too many politicians forgot that. They forgot who sent them to Washington, and who they work for.
So here’s my promise: I’ll work to hold everyone who runs our government, members of Congress, the President, and federal judges alike, to the same higher standard. No exceptions, no carve-outs, no special treatment. Because the government will never work for the rest of us until the people running it answer to us.
Ban Politicians from Trading Stocks
The fastest way to start rebuilding trust is to stop letting the people who write the laws make money on the outcome. We’ve watched members of Congress, the President, cabinet members, and well-connected insiders turn hundreds of thousands, sometimes millions, of dollars in stock trades or prediction markets while sitting on information the rest of us will never see. Some of them are trading on the very decisions they’re making in office. That’s not investing. That’s cheating, and it should be a crime. I support a full ban on stock trading by any member of Congress, the White House, and their staff, so no one in government can pad their own bank account on the public’s dime. And if fines won’t get the job done, we should throw the offenders in jail.
Elected office is not a lifetime appointment. When someone holds the same seat for 20 or 30 years, they stop listening to the people back home and start listening to the lobbyists down the hall. I’ve already written term-limit legislation in Iowa, and I’ll do it again in Congress: a 12-year cap: six House terms or two Senate terms.
A Real Code of Ethics for the Supreme Court
Every federal judge, every Congressperson, and the President is bound by a code of conduct. The most powerful court in the country is not. Supreme Court justices answer to no one but themselves, and it shows. We need a clear, enforceable ethics code: justices step aside when they have a financial stake in a case, full disclosure of every gift and free trip, and an independent body with the power to actually enforce the rules. The Court needs to be accountable to the American people, and we deserve a Court they can trust again.
End Partisan Gerrymandering
Gerrymandering lets politicians pick their voters instead of voters picking their politicians. It’s one of the biggest reasons Washington stopped listening. Iowa figured out a better way decades ago. A nonpartisan agency draws our maps based on population and geography — not party, not incumbents, not who won last time. Politicians can vote a map up or down, but they can’t rig it. I’ll push to ban partisan gerrymandering nationwide and put voters back in charge of their own elections.
Ban Corporate PAC Money
Too many members of Congress spend more time answering to their donors than the people who elected them. Zach Nunn is a perfect example. He’s taken millions from corporate PACs. When that much of your money comes from corporate interests, Iowans have every right to ask who you’re really working for. I haven’t taken a dime from corporate PACs in this race, and I’ll work to ban them outright. The only people your representative should answer to are the ones who sent them there.
Get Rid of Super PACs and Overturn Citizens United
Super PACs are another way corporations and billionaires buy their way around the rules. They pour unlimited, often secret money into our elections. You don’t have to look far to see it. Elon Musk’s America PAC spent $817,700 to get Zach Nunn elected in 2024. Then Nunn turned around and voted to cut Musk’s taxes. That’s the whole game, right there in front of our eyes. I’ll work to ban super PACs and overturn Citizens United, because our democracy should belong to the people, not to whoever writes the biggest check.
A Lifetime Ban on Members of Congress Becoming Lobbyists
Right now, a member of Congress can walk out of office on Friday and start lobbying their old colleagues on Monday, selling the access and connections they built on the taxpayer’s dime to the highest corporate bidder. The moment you start auditioning for your next job, you stop doing the one you have. I’ll push for a lifetime ban on members of Congress becoming lobbyists. Serving the public should never be a steppingstone to cashing in on it.
Required Annual Public Town Halls
The only way to represent people is to actually show up and listen to them, even the ones who didn’t vote for you. Here in Iowa, I’ve held open town halls and knocked on thousands of doors to do exactly that. Zach Nunn hasn’t held a single public town hall during his tenure in Congress. He’s too afraid to stand in a room with the people he represents and answer for his votes. It’s cowardly, and it’s wrong. I’ll push to require every member of Congress to hold open, public town halls every year. If you can’t face the people you serve, you shouldn’t have the job. If members of Congress don’t hold town halls, they shouldn’t get paid.
Put Your Schedule Out in the Open
Iowans deserve to know who has their representative’s ear. Too often, the people getting face time in Washington are lobbyists and big donors, while regular folks can’t even get a call back. I’ll push to require members of Congress to publish a regular public schedule, including their meetings. If a meeting can’t stand the light of day, it probably shouldn’t be happening.
Audit How Washington Spends Your Money
Every dollar the federal government spends is a dollar that comes out of someone’s paycheck. People have a right to know it’s being spent wisely and honestly. I’ll push for regular, independent audits of how federal agencies spend taxpayer dollars, with the results made public for everyone to see. We work hard for that money. The least Washington can do is account for every penny of it.

pages.title: Protecting Iowa’s land, water, and clean energy future - Sarah for Iowa
pages.text:
## Protecting Iowa’s land, water, and clean energy future
Our family farms, open spaces, and rivers are part of what makes Iowa special—and they’re under threat. I’ve worked with conservation groups across the state to protect clean water and expand access to public lands. As the Izaak Walton League’s Legislator of the Year, I’ve seen how bipartisan support can create meaningful change. In Congress, I’ll support investments in clean energy like wind, solar, and biofuels—which already power thousands of Iowa jobs—and I’ll work with farmers to promote sustainable practices that keep our soil healthy and our water safe. We can tackle climate change and strengthen our economy at the same time.

pages.title: Serving our veterans like they served us - Sarah for Iowa
pages.text:
## Serving our veterans like they served us
Our veterans kept their promise to our country. In return, we need to keep our promises to them. I’ve heard from too many veterans in Iowa who are stuck waiting for appointments, denied the mental health support they need, or lost in a maze of bureaucracy. In Congress, I’ll work to expand access to VA services—especially in rural areas—and ensure our vets can access housing, education, and job training without jumping through hoops. I’ll also advocate for increased investment in suicide prevention and crisis response. Supporting veterans is our obligation.

pages.title: Rep. Zach Nunn’s record doesn’t match his rhetoric on tariffs and trade - Sarah for Iowa
pages.text:
Oct 5, 2026
## Rep. Zach Nunn’s record doesn’t match his rhetoric on tariffs and trade
Nunn has had multiple chances to vote down Trump’s tariffs.
Since President Donald Trump announced that US Rep. Zach Nunn (IA-03) would seek re-election instead of running for governor, the Ankeny Republican has had multiple opportunities to make clear his position on tariffs.
- September 2025: Favored tariffs. In September 2025, House Republicans passed a measure blocking challenges to President Donald Trump’s global tariffs. Nunn voted for it.
- Feb. 10, 2026: Favored tariffs. On Feb. 10, Nunn voted for a rule that would have barred fast-track floor votes to end Trump’s emergency tariffs until July 31. In practical effect, this was a vote to prevent the House from acting against the tariffs.
- Feb. 11, 2026: Favored tariffs. On Feb. 11, Nunn voted no on a resolution to end the national emergency Trump used as the legal basis for tariffs on Canadian goods.
- Feb. 13, 2026: Mixed. Nunn was asked by Iowa PBS about the impacts of President Donald Trump’s tariffs on Iowa’s farm economy. Nunn said he supported Trump “holding offenders accountable,” defended tariffs as leverage, and cited trade gains. But he added, “I don’t want to see tariffs used viciously, and I still believe that the first article of the Constitution says that Congress should be leading this.”
Nunn argued that tariffs have actually delivered for Iowa Agriculture.
“What tariffs have brought us on the good side for [agriculture] is 24 million metric tons of soybeans being sent to China,” Nunn said to Iowa PBS.
A Starting Line fact check found that Nunn’s statement isn’t entirely accurate—and the situation isn’t so simple. China has committed to buy 25 million metric tons of US soybeans a year through 2028, but Chinese state-run companies had purchased about 13.7 million metric tons by late September—well short of the 24 million metric tons Nunn said were being sent to China.
Those purchases also came after US-China trade talks and a buying agreement, making it hard to credit tariffs. China stopped buying US crops for months during the tariff dispute, and its remaining 10% tariff on American beans has kept many private Chinese buyers turning instead to Brazil and Argentina.
## China
Nunn’s work on China has intersected with farm policy in ways that raise questions about competing priorities. In February 2025, Nunn was named to the House committee charged with examining China’s economic and national-security influence. That role casts new light on his earlier support for the EATS Act—a bill that would have blocked California from enforcing animal welfare rules on pork sold in the state.
The bill grew out of California’s Proposition 12, which requires pork sold there to meet minimum space standards for breeding pigs, no matter where the animal was raised. Because California buys a major portion of the nation’s pork, Iowa producers who want to access that market have to follow those rules.
One month after the Supreme Court upheld Prop 12 in a 5-4 decision, US Rep. Ashley Hinson, the current Republican candidate for US Senate in Iowa, introduced the EATS Act, and Nunn co-sponsored it.
Opposition to the bill came from the Republican party’s own right flank.
Ten conservative House members wrote they were “gravely concerned about the infiltration of American pork production by foreign adversaries.”
“Smithfield Foods, which controls an extraordinary 26% stake of US pig production and publicly supports the EATS Act, is wholly owned by the [Chinese Communist Party],” the letter said.
Smithfield Foods is majority-owned by WH Group, a publicly traded Hong Kong company.
Separately, the director of Harvard Law School’s Animal Law and Policy Program warned the bill could backfire on Iowa pork producers by stripping state disease protections. The bill did not pass.
That tension showed up again in Nunn’s approach to soybeans.
In October 2025, he urged Trump administration officials to remove retaliatory tariffs and find new markets for Iowa crops, writing that trade friction had priced US soybeans out of China. Later, Nunn credited tariffs with bringing soybean sales back to China.
## The money
Nunn has warned that China can use trade to put pressure on Iowa farmers. But his campaign and leadership PACs have accepted $18,750 since 2021 from the corporate PACs of Syngenta and Smithfield, two agricultural companies with Chinese ownership and US farmland holdings, according to Federal Election Commission records.
Syngenta is owned by Sinochem, a Chinese state-owned company. Smithfield is majority-owned by Hong Kong-based WH Group, which says it is not a Chinese state-owned enterprise.
Democratic challenger Sarah Trone Garriott does not accept corporate PAC contributions.
This article was written by Robert Gundran and was originally published on Iowa Starting Line.
